articles.author: Imran Ahmed
articles.description:
The Retry Storm Problem: How Idempotency Keys Save Your ASP.NET Core API



  
  
  Introduction


Every .NET developer knows the frustration of a failed request followed by an automatic retry. But there's a subtler danger: when those retries hit side-effecting endpoints (payment processing, email dispatch, inventory updates), you can end up with duplicate charges, duplicate notifications, or corrupted state. This is the "retry storm" problem—and it's solved with idempotency keys.
Consider a mobile client that experiences a brief network glitch while placing an order. The HTTP request times out, the client library retries, and because our API doesn't track whether an operation has already been executed, both attempts succeed. The result: the payment gateway charges the card twice, the noti…
articles.title: The Retry Storm Problem: Why Your ASP.NET Core API Needs Idempotency Keys

articles.author: Andy Stanly
articles.description:
I was brushing my teeth on a Tuesday morning, phone propped on the cistern, when the idea dropped: a better title for Sunday's sermon. I opened the app, started a note on Matthew 11, and saved. The phone had been offline since the previous night — patchy signal in the flat, nothing unusual. The app queued the write locally and I forgot about it.
At my desk, forty minutes later, I opened the same note on the laptop and rewrote the first line. Different angle. Then the phone reconnected.
The conflict lasted eleven seconds of user-visible weirdness and about four hours of my week. What it actually exposed was a decision I'd made eighteen months earlier, on purpose, and written down in a comment I still agree with. The decision was: the last write wins, and the clock decides what's last.
That …
articles.title: The last-write-wins clock was wrong, and I wrote it

articles.author: Tamiz Uddin
articles.description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.
In the early hype cycle of generative AI, the prestige move for developers was crafting the perfect prompt—the clever incantation that coaxed a model into producing exactly what you wanted. But as AI moves from demos to production, a new power move is emerging: shipping trustworthy AI artifacts that prove themselves.
This isn’t about prompt engineering anymore. It’s about documentation, provenance, and verifiability. The new frontier of AI reliability is in the artifacts we ship alongside our models: Agent Cards, model manifests, evaluation reports, and behavioral signatures. These aren’t afterthoughts. They’re the foundation of AI systems that can be trusted, audited, and adopted at scale.
Prompt engineering was never a bad skill—it was a necessary one. …
articles.title: From README to Agent Cards: Why Shipping Trustworthy AI Artifacts Beats Clever Prompting

articles.author: Vasim Ahmed Shaikh
articles.description:
CaseMap: Source-Grounded Legal Case Reports You Can Actually Cite


Legal research keeps colliding with the same problem: summaries that paraphrase, invent, or bury the page where a fact actually lives. CaseMap is built to do the opposite — turn a case PDF into a report that stays grounded in the source text, with verbatim quotes and page citations, so you can trust and cite what you read.
Product: https://casemap.ecocodes.in
Showcase: CaseMap on vibecode.law
Demo (video): https://youtu.be/hy4J97sSVpI
You upload or open a case PDF.
CaseMap processes the document and produces a structured case report.
Claims in the report are tied back to exact wording and page numbers from the source — not a free-form rewrite.
That design choice matters for lawyers, researchers, and anyone who cannot afford a hallucinated holding or a soft paraphrase of a statute excerpt.
After processing, CaseMap is built to keep sensitive material browser-local where possible. The goal is useful AI assistance without casually shipping your case files into a black box you cannot audit.
Advocates and in-house counsel who need citeable extracts fast
Researchers comparing holdings across long judgments
Students learning to read cases without losing the page trail
Builders exploring source-grounded document AI (not “chat about a PDF” theater)
CaseMap started as a community / open-minded build around a hard constraint: do not invent, do not paraphrase away the source. If that constraint matches how you work, the live product is here:
→ https://casemap.ecocodes.in
Feedback, bug reports, and “this citation path broke on my PDF” notes are welcome.
Built by Vasim Ahmed Shaikh. Links above are the official CaseMap product and community showcase — use those when you share or cite CaseMap.
articles.title: CaseMap: Source-Grounded Legal Case Reports You Can Actually Cite

That one line from the X pricing page decides the shape of a twitter news bot in Python in 2026: it posts every story to Bluesky and only the best few to X, and "best" has to be a number the script can check. articles.author: Bryan Williams
articles.description:
A practical guide to retries, quote IDs, and the boundary between creating an order and charging for it.
A customer clicks Buy.
Your server creates the order. Before the confirmation reaches the browser, the connection drops.
The customer sees an error and tries again.
Should your server create another order?
That is the problem behind idempotency. The word sounds more complicated than the question: Can we repeat this request without repeating its effect?
In my previous post, I used a revision counter to stop an old response from updating a newer screen. Mike Dabydeen raised the next boundary: what happens when that screen leads to a purchase?
He is right to separate the two. A correct screen does not prove a correct transaction.
Let's start with the practical model, then open up the datab…
articles.title: The Screen Is Correct. Can the Purchase Still Happen Twice?

When I started working on websites and web projects, I noticed something pretty simple.
A website can look completely fine in the browser and still have a lot of small SEO problems.
Maybe the page doesn't have a proper title. Maybe the meta description is missing. Some images don't have alt text. There are broken links. The H1 isn't meaningful. Social metadata or other technical SEO elements might be missing.
None of these problems are particularly difficult to fix, but checking them manually becomes annoying, especially when you're working on multiple pages.
That's what made me build Novash.
Before talking about the tool, it's worth understanding what we're actually trying to check.
SEO isn't just about adding a few keywords to a webpage and hoping Google ranks it.
